You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages and subagent reports are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used and the subagents running. When you have nothing to do until a subagent report or a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `read_file`: read a file with line numbers.
- `list_dir`: list a directory tree.
- `search`: search file contents with a regular expression.
- `spawn_subagents`: start subagents in the background (see Subagents below); it returns at once and each report arrives as a message.
- `wait`: pause until a subagent report or a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).

You cannot run commands or change files yourself: everything that runs a command or modifies the container (building, testing, verifying included) must be delegated with `spawn_subagents`.
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /luxon.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.
- A request to forget or undo an earlier bug: do what it asks, and reply to its id with `done: true` once that code is as the user wants it.

## Subagents
`spawn_subagents(instructions)` takes a list of instructions and starts one subagent per instruction in the background; the call returns at once. Subagents are separate model instances running in the SAME container as you. Each starts fresh: it sees only its instruction, not your conversation or the task, so make every instruction self-contained (goal, paths, commands, constraints, what to report). Each runs at most 2000 steps; its written report arrives as a message when it finishes, and you keep working (or `wait`) meanwhile. They share the filesystem with you and with each other, so give them independent work that does not edit the same files.

Stay available to the user: new messages reach you only between your steps, so every long step, long thinking included, keeps the user waiting. Keep each step short. Do not work out a bug yourself before handing it off: as soon as a bug arrives, start a subagent with a short instruction (the user's bug report as given, the repository path, and what to report back). The subagent can read the code and work out what the problem is and how to fix it on its own. Then reply to the user and go back to waiting.

Scope: hard: subagents have `read_file`, `list_dir`, `search`, `bash` and `edit_file`; they can implement changes and verify them by running tests.

Limits: at most 60 subagents run at once; instructions beyond the free slots are not run. At most 60 subagent runs per episode; the budget left is shown after each step.

## Accessors

Luxon DateTimes have a few different accessors that let you find out about the zone and offset:

```js
var dt = DateTime.local();

dt.zoneName; //=> 'America/New_York'
dt.offset; //=> -240
dt.offsetNameShort; //=> 'EDT'
dt.offsetNameLong; //=> 'Eastern Daylight Time'
dt.isOffsetFixed; //=> false
dt.isInDST; //=> true
```

Those are all documented in the [DateTime API docs](../class/src/datetime.js~DateTime.html).

## DST weirdness

Because our ancestors were morons, they opted for a system wherein many governments shift around the local time twice a year for no good reason. And it's not like they do it in a neat, coordinated fashion. No, they do it whimsically, varying the shifts' timing from country to country (or region to region!) and from year to year. And of course, they do it the opposite way south of the Equator. This is all a tremendous waste of everyone's energy and, er, time, but it is how the world works and a date and a time library has to deal with it.

Most of the time, DST shifts will happen without you having to do anything about it and everything will just work. Luxon goes to some pains to make DSTs as unweird as possible. But there are exceptions. This section covers them.

### Invalid times

Some local times simply don't exist. The Spring Forward DST shift involves shifting the local time forward by (usually) one hour. In my zone, `America/New_York`, on March 12, 2017 the millisecond after 1:59:59.999 is 3:00:00.000. Thus the times between 2:00:00.000 and 2:59:59.000, inclusive, don't exist in that zone. But of course, nothing stops a user from constructing a DateTime out of that local time.

If you create such a DateTime from scratch, the missing time will be advanced by an hour:

```js
DateTime.local(2017, 3, 12, 2, 30).toString(); //=> '2017-03-12T03:30:00.000-04:00'
```

arguments.report:
## Root cause

The bug is in `objToLocalTS` in `/luxon/src/impl/util.js` (not `untruncateYear`; that helper is only used for 2-digit-year parsing and is fine). `objToLocalTS` builds a timestamp with `Date.UTC(...)`, and because JS maps years 0–99 to 19XX, it then "untruncates" the year. The old code did:

```js
d = new Date(d);
d.setUTCFullYear(d.getUTCFullYear() - 1900);
```

`Date.UTC(99, ...)` computes month/day using year **1999/2000**, and 2000 is a leap year while year 100 is not. When an out-of-range day rolls the intermediate date to/after Feb 29 2000 (e.g. `0099-12-31 + 61 days` → intermediate `2000-03-01`), the leap day is baked in; subtracting 1900 then yields a date that is **one day too early** for every day at/after that point in year 100. This is exactly what `DateTime#plus` hits: `adjustTime` calls `objToLocalTS` with `{year: 99, month: 12, day: 31+n}`.

Reproduced: `DateTime.fromISO("0099-12-31").plus({ day: 62 })` returned `0100-03-02` (expected `0100-03-03`); `plus({ days: 61 })` returned `0100-03-01` (expected `0100-03-02`). Also affects `minus` in the reverse direction and `DateTime.fromObject` for low years.

## Fix (git diff of src/impl/util.js)

```diff
@@ -166,7 +166,11 @@ export function objToLocalTS(obj) {
   // for legacy reasons, years between 0 and 99 are interpreted as 19XX; revert that
   if (obj.year < 100 && obj.year >= 0) {
     d = new Date(d);
-    d.setUTCFullYear(d.getUTCFullYear() - 1900);
+    // set the month and day again, this is necessary because year 2000 is a leap year, but year 100 is not
+    // so if obj.year is in 99, but obj.day makes it roll over into year 100,
+    // the calculations done by Date.UTC are using year 2000 - which is a leap year
+    // so we need to set the month and day again
+    d.setUTCFullYear(obj.year, obj.month - 1, obj.day);
   }
   return +d;
 }
```

Re-applying the original (possibly out-of-range) month/day with the true year makes the JS engine normalize using year 99/100 rules, so no spurious leap day is introduced.

Temp test `test/datetime/tmp_barrier.test.js` (created, used, **deleted** — confirmed absent):
- Before fix: `DateTime.fromISO("0099-12-31").plus({ day: 62 })` → `0100-03-02` (FAIL, expected 03-03); same failure with `fromObject({year:99,month:12,day:31}).plus({months:2,days:3})`.
- After fix: both pass. ## Root cause

The bug is in `objToLocalTS` in `/luxon/src/impl/util.js` (not `untruncateYear`; that helper is only used for 2-digit-year parsing and is fine). `objToLocalTS` builds a timestamp with `Date.UTC(...)`, and because JS maps years 0–99 to 19XX, it then "untruncates" the year. The old code did:

```js
d = new Date(d);
d.setUTCFullYear(d.getUTCFullYear() - 1900);
```

`Date.UTC(99, ...)` computes month/day using year **1999/2000**, and 2000 is a leap year while year 100 is not. When an out-of-range day rolls the intermediate date to/after Feb 29 2000 (e.g. `0099-12-31 + 61 days` → intermediate `2000-03-01`), the leap day is baked in; subtracting 1900 then yields a date that is **one day too early** for every day at/after that point in year 100. This is exactly what `DateTime#plus` hits: `adjustTime` calls `objToLocalTS` with `{year: 99, month: 12, day: 31+n}`.

Reproduced: `DateTime.fromISO("0099-12-31").plus({ day: 62 })` returned `0100-03-02` (expected `0100-03-03`); `plus({ days: 61 })` returned `0100-03-01` (expected `0100-03-02`). Also affects `minus` in the reverse direction and `DateTime.fromObject` for low years.

## Fix (git diff of src/impl/util.js)

```diff
@@ -166,7 +166,11 @@ export function objToLocalTS(obj) {
   // for legacy reasons, years between 0 and 99 are interpreted as 19XX; revert that
   if (obj.year < 100 && obj.year >= 0) {
     d = new Date(d);
-    d.setUTCFullYear(d.getUTCFullYear() - 1900);
+    // set the month and day again, this is necessary because year 2000 is a leap year, but year 100 is not
+    // so if obj.year is in 99, but obj.day makes it roll over into year 100,
+    // the calculations done by Date.UTC are using year 2000 - which is a leap year
+    // so we need to set the month and day again
+    d.setUTCFullYear(obj.year, obj.month - 1, obj.day);
   }
   return +d;
 }
```

Re-applying the original (possibly out-of-range) month/day with the true year makes the JS engine normalize using year 99/100 rules, so no spurious leap day is introduced.

function fixOffset(localTS, o, tz) {

  let utcGuess = localTS - o * 60 * 1000;

  if (o === o2) {

  // If not, change the ts by the difference in the offset

  if (o2 === o3) {

  }

  // If it's different, we're in a hole time. The offset has changed, but the we don't adjust the time
  return [localTS - Math.min(o2, o3) * 60 * 1000, Math.max(o2, o3)];
}
